title: AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

reading.body:
This is a case of a generative AI model asserting fabricated information as fact, a failure mode commonly called hallucination. An AI tool called Irys was used to assist in preparing legal filings, and it produced seven case citations across eight filings that do not exist, along with incorrect case titles and false quotes attributed to those cases. The error was not caught before submission, meaning no human verification of the cited sources occurred at the point where the filings were finalized.

The failure happened at the drafting stage of litigation, a deployment context that requires every cited authority to be independently verifiable. Catching it would have required a lawyer to look up each citation in an authoritative legal database before filing, which is standard practice when research is done by hand. The use of an AI tool did not trigger that check, or the check was skipped.

What is not established is whether the court has yet imposed any sanction, what the outcome of the underlying lawsuit will be, or whether the fabricated citations materially affected any ruling in the case.

reports.title: State Farm defense lawyers admit AI generated fake cases in LA lawsuit
AI hallucinated case law in insurance company’s filings in L.A. County house fire dispute
AI Hallucinations in State Farm Insurance Outside Lawyers' Filings

summary:
# Summary

State Farm's lawyers apologized after admitting they used artificial intelligence to prepare legal filings in a Los Angeles lawsuit, and the AI generated fake court cases, nonexistent quotes, and false legal holdings. The case involves homeowner Fa'alagilagi Meni-Siliga, who is suing State Farm and others after a 2020 fire destroyed her Carson home. While repairs were underway, storm damage occurred, and Meni-Siliga claims State Farm delayed approving additional repairs, leaving the work incomplete. She and her husband exhausted their savings, declared bankruptcy, and lost their home to foreclosure. State Farm's lawyer Jacquelene Robinson acknowledged using an AI tool called Irys and confirmed seven case citations across eight filings did not actually exist, along with incorrect case titles and false quotes.

The incident reflects a growing problem in the legal industry, where 41 percent of law firms now use generative AI. A Stanford law professor noted that legal AI hallucinations are becoming increasingly common, and a Paris-based researcher's database has recorded 1,922 cases of AI-generated legal errors worldwide, mostly in the United States. Last year, another California attorney received a record ten thousand dollar fine for using ChatGPT in a brief containing 21 fabricated quotes. The Meni-Siliga case is scheduled for trial in October.
